paper_title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A few seconds can capture moment, but story needs time to unfold. MovieRoll Team Visual generative models now support realistic video synthesis [1, 21, 24, 25, 38, 41, 50, 59, 62, 67, 82, 83], synchronized audio-visual generation [25, 36], and increasingly flexible content control [20, 39, 42, 72, 79]. Work done during internship at Tencent Hunyuan 1 Figure 1 MovieRoll generates minute-long video with continuous subject identity across six events. The sequence shows the same woman performing successive actions in one studio setting, with new prompt every 10s. Each frame represents one event, and the text below summarizes its prompt. However, bidirectional video models jointly denoise the full sequence, delaying the first output and increasing computation as duration grows. Streaming generation instead produces chunks sequentially from previously generated content [5, 27, 28, 32, 56, 65, 71, 76, 78], enabling continuous output and online interaction. Sustaining quality over long sequences remains challenging. With teacher forcing, models learn from short videos conditioned on ground-truth history. At inference, the shift to self-generated history introduces exposure bias, while longer generation requires extrapolation beyond the training horizon. Growing KV caches further increase memory and computation costs. Self Forcing [29] addresses exposure bias through self-rollout distillation, and LongLive [65] extends this approach to long sequences. These approaches primarily target few-step generators, leaving capable multi-step streaming bases less explored. Resampling Forcing [23] and Helios-Base [73] address multi-step generation, but the former evaluates durations up to 15s, while the latter uses bidirectional continuation without KV caching. History management introduces further tradeoffs. Sliding windows discard intermediate context [29, 45, 65, 85], while retrieval [3], evolving memory [2], and context compression [9, 68] introduce additional mechanisms. We present MovieRoll, base-to-distilled framework that builds multi-step base through streaming finetuning and few-step generator through long self-rollouts. As illustrated in Fig. 1, MovieRoll supports longform generation with sequential event prompts. At the base stage, Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF) adapts pretrained bidirectional model using rolling windows [45, 52, 58]. Each window jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention and causal access to preceding clean history. Parallel window training improves long-horizon robustness over chunk-wise training. Hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) retains full history in shallow layers and only sinkrecent history in deeper layers. Compared with full-history caching across all layers, it reduces KV-cache memory by up to 78% and peak denoising-step latency with CFG by approximately 53%, while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) trains few-step generator on long self-rollouts under DMD supervision [69, 70]. Whereas LongLive-style training updates from individual supervision windows, CuLT-DMD holds parameters fixed throughout each rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update combines supervision across time, keeping one local computation graph at time and improving long-horizon generation over LongLive-style training. At inference, threshold-triggered history selection and KV recomputation rebuild the cache from representative generated chunks for both MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled, bounding the retained context and improving extrapolation beyond the training horizon. Classifier-free guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) further stabilizes MovieRoll-Base by reducing guidance strength [26] toward the clean endpoint, limiting late-stage extrapolation before generated chunks become history. The Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill expresses sustained actions and maintains shared entities across event prompts. MovieRoll also provides infrastructure for efficient training and streaming output. Flash Block-wise Causal Attention (FBCA) packs visible keys and values for FlashAttention, accelerating window-parallel training across input shapes. Parallel Streaming VAE (PS-VAE) preserves temporal state across decoded chunks and distributes spatial computation across devices, lowering latency and memory use for incremental decoding. On HeliosBench [73], MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s. MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods for single-event generation at 10s, 30s, and 60s and multi-event generation at 30s and 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion. user study further shows majority preference for MovieRoll-Distilled over every evaluated baseline in both settings. In summary, MovieRoll makes four contributions. First, it establishes robust multi-step streaming base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing and HieraKV. Second, it introduces CuLT-DMD to train few-step generator by aggregating supervision across long self-rollouts. Third, it supports long-horizon inference through KV recomputation for both models and AnnealCFG for MovieRoll-Base. Finally, it provides FBCA and PS-VAE for efficient training and streaming decoding.

sections.title: 2.1 Bidirectional Video Generation Models
sections.content: Bidirectional video diffusion jointly denoises latent sequence, allowing each frame to use both past and future context. Together with spatiotemporal compression and large-scale training, this formulation supports highquality video synthesis [38, 41, 59, 62, 67, 82]. Joint refinement lets the model coordinate appearance and motion across the clip throughout denoising. Scaling to longer clips increases attention memory and computation. Hybrid linearsoftmax attention [7] and sparse attention in pretrained video transformers [63, 66] reduce this cost while retaining joint denoising across the clip. complementary direction changes the generation order so that completed chunks can be emitted before the entire sequence is available.

sections.title: 2.2 Autoregressive Video Generation Models
sections.content: To support sequential output, temporal noise schedules separate the denoising progress of different frames. Diffusion Forcing [5] permits independent noise levels, while SkyReels-V2 [6] uses non-decreasing schedules. FIFO-Diffusion [37] applies staggered denoising to frame queue at inference, while Rolling Forcing [45] trains rolling-window generator that jointly refines chunks at ordered noise levels. Robust continuation further benefits from guidance with variable-length history [55] and training with corrupted history [73]. Few-step distillation reduces per-chunk latency, as demonstrated by CausVid [71], Helios-Distilled [73], and Krea-Realtime [47]. Beyond distribution matching objectives [69, 70], initialization and rollout exposure shape generation quality. Causal Forcing [85] uses an autoregressive teacher for ODE initialization, while Self Forcing [29] trains on self-generated histories. For longer rollouts, LongLive [65] applies DMD supervision to each newly generated clip. Self-Forcing++ [13] uses short-video teacher to supervise sampled segments of long self-generated videos. Context Forcing [9] additionally gives the teacher access to long-range history. Using longer context also raises the cost of storing and processing history. Temporal pyramids [35] and coarser tokens for distant frames [22] reduce the historical token count, while block linear attention accumulates fixed-size state [8]. Within KV caches, compression can follow the distinct roles of layers and heads. PyramidKV [4] varies cache allocation across language-model layers. In video models, head-specific pruning [34] and calibrated layerhead token merging [61] adapt compression to attention structure.

sections.title: 2.3 Interactive Video Generation Models
sections.content: Beyond sustaining sequence, interactive generation must respond to changing user input while preserving scene continuity. Applications range from navigable environments [48, 57] to camera-controlled video [84]. For streaming video, history management must therefore account for the active condition as well as memory cost. LongLive [65] retains recent frames and persistent sink, refreshing cached KV states under the new 3 Figure 2 Overview of MovieRoll. Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF) trains MovieRoll-Base through parallel window supervision conditioned on clean history and event prompts. After ODE initialization, Cumulative Long Tuning with Distribution Matching Distillation (CuLT-DMD) trains few-step generator by averaging local gradients across long self-rollouts. Both models jointly denoise rolling window, use hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) to retain history across layers, and rebuild the cache at history threshold or prompt switch. Classifier-free guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) gradually reduces guidance during base-model denoising. prompt at prompt switches. For sink-based histories, LoL [14] uses multi-head RoPE jitter to reduce repeated returns to sink-frame content. Adaptive memory policies retrieve prompt-relevant history [33] or learn an evolving memory as frames leave the local window [2]. Meeting interactive latency targets requires both model and system design. On-policy distillation enables fast multimodal avatar generation [10], while deadline-aware scheduling reduces delays in live streams [19]. SANA-Streaming [80] combines model and system optimization for temporally consistent video editing.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: MovieRoll jointly denoises rolling window of latent chunks at progressively increasing noise levels. Fully denoised chunks are emitted, and their KV states are cached for subsequent generation. Attention is bidirectional within the active window and causal with respect to fully denoised historical chunks. As outlined in Fig. 2, we first adapt pretrained bidirectional video model into MovieRoll-Base using Windowwise Teacher Forcing (WinTF). Each training pass supervises multiple windows conditioned on preceding ground-truth chunks and event-specific prompts, enabling MovieRoll-Base to learn transitions across events. We initialize five-step student using ODE trajectories from MovieRoll-Base, then train it on long selfgenerated rollouts using Cumulative Long Tuning with DMD (CuLT-DMD). frozen bidirectional model provides real-score estimates. CuLT-DMD updates the generator with local gradients accumulated over each rollout. At inference, HieraKV stores all available historical KV states in shallow blocks and retains only sinkrecent history in deeper blocks. Threshold-triggered KV recomputation periodically rebuilds the historical KV cache from selected fully denoised chunks. AnnealCFG decreases the guidance scale during MovieRoll-Base denoising. The Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill converts user instructions into descriptions of ongoing actions and consistent entities for single-event and multi-event generation.

sections.title: 3.3 HieraKV: Hierarchical KV-Cache Compression across Layers
sections.content: Full-history KV caching incurs increasing memory and computation costs as video length grows, whereas uniform sliding-window caching discards intermediate history at every layer. Our inference-time analysis of the WinTF-trained model shows that attention to history varies with network depth, as illustrated in Fig. 4. Shallow blocks distribute attention relatively evenly across historical chunks, while deeper blocks concentrate more attention on sink and recent chunks. Historical-attention entropy also decreases modestly with depth. Guided by these attention patterns, HieraKV varies history retention across depth. The first Ls blocks retain all available historical KV states, while deeper blocks cache only the sink chunk and the most recent historical chunk. The sink anchors visual content, and recent history provides immediate temporal context. Intermediate history remains accessible through the shallow-block outputs, while the active window retains bidirectional attention at every depth.

sections.title: 3.6 Threshold-Triggered KV Recomputation for Extrapolation
sections.content: Streaming video models are trained with finite historical contexts but often need to generate beyond that horizon. Retaining all KV states increases memory usage and computational cost while exposing the model to longer contexts than those seen during training. Sliding-window extrapolation limits KV cache growth, but retained KV states may still depend on previously attended chunks that have since been evicted [47], as illustrated in Fig. 7. When history reaches configured threshold, we retain the sink chunk, representative event-middle chunks, and recent chunks. causal-attention forward pass re-encodes them in temporal order at = 0, without text conditioning. Generation resumes from this rebuilt cache, bounding storage and removing cached dependencies on discarded chunks. Event-prompt switches also trigger recomputation.

sections.title: 3.7 Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill
sections.content: Streaming generation requires sustained actions and consistent entities across prompts. Instructions with natural endpoints, such as zoom-in, can be difficult to sustain over long sequences. 9 Figure 8 Flash Block-wise Causal Attention (FBCA) implements block-causal attention with efficient FlashAttention kernels. Each query block gathers its visible prefix, historical states, and current states into an independent attention sequence. KV unfolding and grouping organize these sequences within per-call packing budget, and variable-length FlashAttention processes them before restoring the original block order. This preserves the required attention pattern while controlling the size of each packed buffer. Our Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill expands short user instructions into sustained actions and consistent scene descriptions. For single-event generation, it develops the action within one scene. For multi-event generation, it uses preceding rewritten prompts to maintain continuity. See App. for details.

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: MovieRoll-Base is initialized from HunyuanVideo-1.5-480P-T2V [62] with 6 full-history and 48 sinkrecent blocks. During decoding, the rolling window contains five chunks of four latent frames each. During streaming fine-tuning, we perturb clean histories with probability = 0.9 and noise level σ U(0, 0.15). MovieRollDistilled undergoes ODE initialization followed by CuLT-DMD on singleand two-event prompts. All stages use Muon [44]. At inference, MovieRoll-Base uses 50 steps with CFG annealed from 4 to 1, while MovieRollDistilled uses five steps without CFG. Both use an Euler solver with timestep shift of 5 and KV recomputation threshold of 18 chunks. App. provides the full configurations. We evaluate 200 randomly sampled single-event prompts from MovieGen [50] and VBench [30, 81] category sets. Multi-event evaluation uses 100 MemFlow [33] prompts. We use our Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill to rewrite all single-event and multi-event evaluation prompts. Video evaluation spans visual quality, temporal consistency, and prompt alignment [31]. We report all HeliosBench metrics [73]. The evaluators use CLIP [51] for aesthetics, Farnebäck optical flow [18] for dynamics, AMT-S [40] for motion smoothness, and ViCLIP [60] for semantic alignment. Naturalness is evaluated with three Gemini-2.5-Pro [12] queries per video. Multi-event semantic and drifting-semantic scores are averaged across events. App. details the evaluation protocol.

sections.title: 6.1 Conclusion
sections.content: MovieRoll connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference in base-todistilled framework. WinTF establishes robust multi-step streaming base, and CuLT-DMD builds on it to train few-step generator through supervision across long self-rollouts. HieraKV and KV recomputation retain historical context efficiently for both models, while AnnealCFG further stabilizes MovieRoll-Base. FBCA and PS-VAE complement these methods with efficient training and streaming decoding. Together, these designs enable competitive 30s generation from MovieRoll-Base despite training on videos of up to 15s. MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total HeliosBench scores among the compared methods across singleand multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.

sections.title: 7.1 Agentic Streaming Generation
sections.content: In our experience, streaming models approach bidirectional quality in visually constrained settings, such as digital-human animation and game-world scenes with limited visual variation, but struggle with complex motion and camera trajectories. Difficulty maintaining continuity as instructions change may contribute to this gap. Even with fixed prompt, an unfolding event can leave the next action unspecified. These challenges motivate generation guided by both user intent and the current visual state. An agent could provide this guidance by observing newly generated frames and translating user instructions into successive events. It could update the active prompt as the scene develops and plan transitions when new instructions conflict with existing objects or states. Such planning would connect immediate instructions to the generated history while preserving compatible scene content. The Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill in Sec. 3.7 provides starting point through its rules for event organization and textual continuity. Visual feedback could extend this process by guiding revisions to the event plan during generation. To support these finer adjustments, window-level captions could complement 29 (a) Smaller chunks allow finer noise Figure 27 Potential extensions of rolling-window video pretraining. progression and temporal advances at fixed frame budget, while loss weighting or regularization could balance learning across noise levels. (b) Total-duration conditioning could guide overall pacing, while duration triggers locate active windows and shot transitions. Together with multi-shot training, these conditions could support coordinated shot sequences under one prompt. event-level conditions with supervision for local actions and state changes.

sections.title: 7.2 Pretraining Foundation Models for Autoregressive Video Generation
sections.content: Agentic control also calls for model that can continue an evolving scene under changing conditions. MovieRoll adapts pretrained bidirectional video model for streaming generation. Native autoregressive pretraining would align the model with this setting from the outset and allow us to study whether temporal causal attention can match bidirectional visual quality under comparable data and compute budgets. This direction could build on language-model infrastructure while retaining bidirectional attention within each active chunk or window. Optimized kernels can skip temporally masked interactions, with savings determined by the chunk or window size and kernel implementation. At inference, KV caching could reuse fully denoised history as the model repeatedly denoises the active video tokens. common conditional interface could then support text-to-video, image-to-video, and continuation with shared backbone. Adding source videos, masks, and control inputs would extend the same framework to video transformation, inpainting, and controlled generation. Joint pretraining would let us study how data diversity, model capacity, and context length affect quality and transfer. Across these tasks, shared temporal attention rules would connect training to inference, while robustness to self-generated history would remain learning objective for maintaining continuity over extended video rollouts. WinTF offers starting point for this training framework, as its ablation shows better preservation of longhorizon quality than chunk-wise teacher forcing in Tab. 5. Building on this result, Fig. 27 outlines two connected directions. Rolling-window optimization would address how generation advances through time, while explicit temporal conditions would specify its pace and shot structure. Finer Noise Levels with Smaller Chunks. At fixed active-frame budget, using more, smaller chunks would allow denser noise progression and finer temporal advances. The chunk adjacent to clean history could therefore lie closer to the clean endpoint. Greater overlap between consecutive windows could further smooth the transition from clean history to noisy content and improve continuation. Regularization for Rolling-Window Losses. Finer noise levels also motivate balancing their contributions to training. Loss weighting or regularization, guided by observed training dynamics, could account for differences in loss scale and optimization progress across the window. Duration Conditioning. In bidirectional training, the temporal extent of the full attention window reveals the target duration, allowing the model to adjust motion speed and content planning accordingly. An autoregressive model sees only the available prefix and active window, which do not specify the total trainingvideo length. Without this global duration cue, it tends to generate at the average motion speed learned for each position across training clips. Because text-to-video generation starts without history, it is biased toward the pacing of short clips, making it difficult to learn duration-dependent behavior from mixed-duration data. total-duration condition would address this ambiguity by pairing each training-window caption with the full video duration. At inference, target duration, or pseudo-duration, would specify the time budget for motion and event planning. While total duration sets the overall time budget, duration trigger would specify where the active window starts and ends and when shot transitions occur. These positions would be expressed as fractions of the total video duration. During training, they would come from the sampled window and observed shot boundaries. At inference, they would come from the current window and specified shot schedule. Multi-Shot Data Training. Multi-shot videos would provide supervision for applying these temporal conditions across changes in viewpoint or scene. shared caption could describe the shots and their order across windows, while the duration trigger would locate transitions within each window. Training on windows that span shot boundaries would allow us to test whether window-wise denoising preserves within-shot content and follows the requested transition times. Together, these temporal conditions could help the agent in Sec. 7.1 translate event plans into paced sequences and shot transitions. Beyond controlling when events occur, longer-term goal is to learn how scenes evolve under different actions, including the physical regularities and causal relationships reflected in diverse motions and interactions. Comparing predicted and observed consequences of different actions from the same initial visual state would provide one way to study this capability.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: Sec. 5.1 summarizes the main training and inference settings. Tab. 8, Tab. 9, and Tab. 10 provide the model configuration and detailed hyperparameters. A.1 Training Data MovieRoll is trained on an internal video corpus that cannot be released publicly because of confidentiality restrictions. Tab. 10 reports the data scale, sample duration, resolution, and task composition for each stage. A.2 Streaming Fine-Tuning We assign increasing timesteps to chunks in temporal order within each rolling window. We first split [0, 1] at sorted random points, then sample shared logit-normal relative position and use it to select raw timestep within each sub-interval. Each raw timestep is shifted to = sq/[1 + (s 1)q] before noising and model conditioning, with = 3 in both streaming fine-tuning stages, as specified in Tab. 10. For each sampled phase, the first window uses up to the available number of chunks, and subsequent windows are full. trailing remainder that cannot fill another window is omitted from that training pass. The flow-matching loss averages over all supervised latent entries. Occasionally, all chunks instead receive the same timestep. We also perturb clean history with noise to approximate the self-generated history encountered at inference. In Stage 2, all chunks in each training window share one prompt. Base-stage clips are bucketed in steps of 8 frames. The batch size per data-parallel group decreases with clip length, from 6 clips at 33 frames to 1 clip at 121 frames. A.3 Streaming Architecture All 54 blocks read clean history from KV cache. The first 6 blocks attend to all retained historical chunks, while the remaining 48 attend to the first chunk, which serves as an attention sink, and the most recent chunk. Within each layer group, cached chunks and the current window are indexed contiguously from zero, keeping temporal RoPE positions bounded as the video grows. A.4 Distillation For ODE initialization, the Stage 2 base model serves as 50-step teacher with CFG linearly annealed from 4 to 1. The 5-step student learns to reproduce the clean endpoints of the rolling teacher trajectories, preserving the annealed guidance behavior with fewer sampling steps. After initialization, CuLT-DMD trains the generator on full videos produced with its 5-step schedule. For each predicted window, we prepend the nearest preceding generated latent frames to form score clip of up to 31 latent frames. If fewer history frames are available, the score clip starts at the video beginning and remains unpadded. Only the current window contributes to the DMD loss. Motivated by the mixed training strategy of Rolling Forcing [45], we regularize predictions across noise levels. With probability 0.5, we re-noise the predicted window at shared timestep and run it through the generator again before computing the local DMD loss. A.5 Inference When the cached history reaches the recomputation threshold, we select chunks and rebuild the KV cache according to Tab. 9. This bounds memory usage and keeps positions within the RoPE range. For multi-event prompts, an event-prompt switch also triggers KV recomputation, with intermediate chunks retained only from the five most recent events. A.6 Ablation Settings The HieraKV quality ablation in Tab. 5 trains each block allocation on the same data for 10K steps using the Stage 1 settings. sections.title: E Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill
sections.content: The system prompt below defines the rewriting interfaces, continuity rules, and validation procedure for the skill in Sec. 3.7. Multi-event evaluation uses the sequential interface with only past and current events. Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill Description. Rewrites short user inputs into structured, single-paragraph prompts for streaming (indefinitely extended) video generation, in single-event and interactive multi-event settings. Goal. Expand short user input into an objective, detailed prompt that describes scene which can be extended chunk by chunk indefinitely, without reaching dead end. Modes. In Single mode, one input sentence one prompt. In Sequential (interactive) mode, given the finalized rewrites of all previous events and one new raw event, rewrite only the new event. Future events are never visible. In Batch mode, known events prompts, separated by @@@EVENT_BREAK@@@. Hard constraints. 1. Camera. Specify exactly one base behavior in single canonical sentence for static camera (The camera remains static, keeping [subject] centered.) or tracking camera (The camera tracks [subject], continuously keeping [subject] centered.). Use tracking when the subject moves through space and static otherwise. Convert any other movement (pan, zoom, dolly, tilt, orbit, crane, roll) to the closer of the two. static camera never reframes. 2. Centering. The main subject stays at the frame center throughout. Close-ups only for stationary subjects. 3. Open-ended action. Describe ongoing or repeating motion. Never use ending words (finally, eventually, in the end, at last, wraps up). After the opening beats, switch to continuity framing (Throughout, Meanwhile). 4. Natural pace. Real-world speed unless the input specifies otherwise. Avoid stacked intensifiers. Summarize crowds instead of animating many small elements. Under static camera the subject must still visibly move (breathing, swaying, gesturing). 5. Fidelity. Keep every entity, exact count, event order, requested style, and on-screen text. Never invent or drop subjects. 6. Style. Default to cinematic realism, also for fantastical subjects, unless the input names another style. End with single short style tag, e.g., Cinematic photography realistic style. 7. Format. Output only the prompt as single paragraph in the present tense, without self-referential phrases (e.g., this video shows). Use the same language as the input. If the language is unclear or unsupported, default to English. Keep the output to 150300 words, or an equivalent length for languages where word counts are not directly comparable. Prompt structure. Summary sentence naming all subjects subject appearance chronological action (Initially / Then / Next Throughout) environment, where every sound has visible source restatement of the subjects fixed traits camera sentence, shot size, lighting, mood style tag. Multi-event consistency. One camera setup (behavior, viewpoint, angle, shot size) for the whole sequence. New subjects enter the established frame. Switch between static and tracking only when an event requires it. Recurring entities keep identical descriptions. The setting stays the same unless the input moves it. Each prompt reintroduces entities without cross-event pronouns, using their full noun phrase (It glides toward the diver. The giant manta ray glides toward the diver in the black wetsuit.). Each event continues from the previous state and receives the full length budget. Validation. Every output is checked automatically for length, single paragraph, ending words, self-reference, forbidden camera motion, exactly one camera sentence, and explicit centering under tracking. Failed outputs are regenerated with the violations appended as feedback, for up to 3 attempts.
